title: A Powerful Way To Relieve Stress: Part One
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In the first entry of a stress-relief series written amid pandemic-era school closures, Michael Linsin argues that teachers under acute, immediate stress need something more powerful than generic lifestyle tips like eating better or journaling. His prescribed remedy is walking, ideally outdoors, for at least an hour at a stretch, done without any push toward exercise performance. He walks through walking's well-documented physical benefits before pivoting to its psychological power: getting outside resets perspective, and sustained, unhurried movement creates the mental distance needed to defuse an overtaxed nervous system. He offers practical guidance on how to walk for this purpose, emphasizing gentle attention to the present moment rather than working through problems, and suggests varying routes to keep the mind engaged. The piece closes with a Kierkegaard quote and a call to action: lace up your shoes and go.
points: Frames walking as an immediate, powerful stress-relief method for a specific kind of acute overwhelm, not just general wellness.
Recommends walking for at least an hour, ideally outdoors in nature, without trying to turn it into a structured workout.
Advises gently redirecting the wandering mind to the present moment rather than using the walk to solve problems.
Suggests varying your route to keep the experience novel, which helps hold attention in the moment.
Notes the cumulative and immune-boosting benefits of daily walking, alongside its capacity to improve sleep.
quotes: My goal isn’t to offer you a few ideas that may or may not be helpful. It isn’t to give you tips like eat more walnuts or stay off social media.

Daily stress is something that feeds on itself and gets worse as time goes on. You may experience brief periods of respite here and there, but because it’s so close to the surface, it overtakes you again and again and at the least provocation.
A word of warning: The methods I’m going to write about in this series may seem extreme. But I promise they work and I’ll make them as gentle and doable as possible.
Now, to enhance all these benefits, both mental and physical, and to experience immediate and often profound relief from stress, I recommend walking for at least an hour.
Instead, focus on enjoying the walk. Inevitably, as soon as you leave your house, your mind will be wound up and trying to work out the areas of your life that are causing your stress.
One trick to help you stay in the moment is to explore. Don’t walk the same familiar path every day.
